lessons.title: Design a repeatable Macrobenchmark
lessons.explanation: Macrobenchmark drives an installed app from a separate benchmark process and measures a user journey on a device. The build, startup mode, compilation state, device and initial data are part of the experiment. Separate setup actions from the measured block so results match the question.
lessons.example: Five illustrative cold-start measurements are 405, 390, 710, 400 and 395 ms. Sorted, their median is 400 ms. A single 390 ms run hides the 710 ms outlier. Compare repeated control and candidate runs, inspect traces and investigate thermal state or unrelated activity before attributing the difference.
lessons.exercise: The candidate was measured after the notes database had warmed; the control also performed its first migration. What would you rerun?
lessons.answer: Measure both variants under the same migration and cache conditions. If first install matters, run a separate first-install journey and label it clearly.

lessons.title: Control compilation with a Baseline Profile
lessons.explanation: A Baseline Profile describes important code paths so ART can compile selected methods ahead of time under supported installation and compilation conditions. It can reduce interpretation or just-in-time compilation on early journeys. It cannot remove an unnecessary network wait or disk access.
lessons.example: A startup trace spends 70 ms executing a hot method and 250 ms waiting for data. Compare otherwise identical builds and device compilation modes with and without the intended profile. Confirm that the startup journey is in the profile, then inspect which trace intervals actually change.
lessons.exercise: Why can comparing a profiled release build against a debug build give the wrong reason for a speedup?
lessons.answer: Compilation, optimization and debug instrumentation all changed. Hold the build type and other inputs constant, explicitly control compilation and compare the same journey.

lessons.title: Name the startup finish line
lessons.explanation: A cold startup begins without an app process. A warm or hot start reuses some prior work. Time to initial display measures the first frame, while time to full display tracks the app’s declaration that meaningful content is ready. Define what useful means for the screen before instrumenting it.
lessons.example: The launch starts at 0 ms. The first frame with placeholders appears at 340 ms. A readable, tappable notes list appears at 920 ms. Recording full display at the placeholder would hide 580 ms. If network data is optional, define whether usable local content satisfies the contract.
lessons.exercise: A release improves first display by 100 ms while full display worsens by 200 ms. Did startup improve?
lessons.answer: The initial frame appeared sooner while useful content arrived later. Report both changes, inspect the first-use path and choose the metric that matches the product promise.

lessons.title: Query trace slices without double counting
lessons.explanation: Perfetto exposes timestamped events as tables. A slice has a name, start timestamp, duration and track. Timestamp and duration in the standard slice table are in nanoseconds. Filter by the correct track and interval before interpreting totals; nested or overlapping slices can double count wall time.
lessons.example: For your own instrumented slice named DecodeThumbnail, start with SELECT track_id, ts, dur / 1000000.0 AS ms FROM slice WHERE name = 'DecodeThumbnail' AND dur >= 0 ORDER BY ts. A parent lasting 18 ms may contain a 12 ms child. Adding them gives 30 ms of labels inside only 18 ms of elapsed parent time.
lessons.exercise: Two decoder tracks each show 15 ms in the same 15 ms interval. Does that prove the UI blocked for 30 ms?
lessons.answer: No. Identify which thread the UI awaited, align events on the timeline and inspect scheduling or dependencies. Concurrent elapsed intervals and nested durations cannot simply be summed into UI latency.

lessons.title: Budget image pixels in bytes
lessons.explanation: A compressed image file and its decoded pixels have different sizes. For a tightly packed 32-bit ARGB bitmap, estimate width × height × 4 bytes before padding and other allocations. Bitmap pixel storage has varied by Android version; native allocations can matter even when the managed wrapper is small.
lessons.example: A 4000 by 3000 image needs about 48,000,000 bytes, or 45.8 MiB, for one tightly packed buffer. Four decoded copies need roughly 183 MiB before temporary buffers. A 1000 by 750 preview needs about 2.86 MiB in the same format. Measure the actual allocation on the target device.
lessons.exercise: The network file shrinks from 2 MB to 1 MB but decode size stays 4000 by 3000. How much did your decoded estimate fall?
lessons.answer: It stayed at about 45.8 MiB for that pixel format. Decode near the display size and bound the number of concurrent images to reduce this cost.

lessons.title: Interpret a low-memory process death
lessons.explanation: System pressure concerns many processes and multiple kinds of memory. Android's low memory killer daemon can terminate less important processes under pressure. Process importance, pressure signals and device policy influence selection; there is no universal app-size threshold that predicts every kill.
lessons.example: After visiting a gallery, an app enters the background and later returns in a new process. Check process identity and available exit evidence, then compare memory across a representative device and workload. A fresh process proves recreation; on its own it does not establish an out-of-memory exception or a leaking Activity.
lessons.exercise: Would raising the app's managed heap limit guarantee the cached process remains alive?
lessons.answer: No. A managed allocation limit and system-wide process reclaim are different boundaries. Reduce dispensable memory and persist the state needed to recover from any process death.

lessons.title: Trim by recovery cost and visibility
lessons.explanation: Classify memory as durable user data, essential working state or rebuildable caches. When the UI is no longer visible, some caches can be reduced or dropped. Android trim callbacks and supported levels vary by API version; correctness must survive even if no warning arrives.
lessons.example: A thumbnail cache occupies 80 MiB and a transient full-size preview holds 46 MiB. Closing the viewer releases the preview. After backgrounding, shrinking the cache to 20 MiB can free another 60 MiB of retained cache entries. Releasing references makes memory eligible for reuse; it does not guarantee an immediate equal fall in reported process size.
lessons.exercise: A draft is stored only inside the thumbnail cache entry. Is clearing it safe under memory pressure?
lessons.answer: Persist the user’s draft independently before eviction. A cache is safe to discard only if its contents can be rebuilt without losing the user’s work.

lessons.title: Distinguish allocation rate from retained growth
lessons.explanation: Allocation tracking records which code creates objects over a selected interval. Heap inspection asks which objects are still reachable at a chosen time. A high allocation rate can create churn, while a low rate can still hide a slow leak. Repeat one controlled interaction to separate the two.
lessons.example: A scroll creates 6,000 temporary objects per second with a mean of 80 bytes: roughly 480,000 bytes per second allocated before overhead. If they become unreachable promptly, retained heap may stay flat. Conversely, retaining a single 4 MiB bitmap per visit grows retained data by about 40 MiB after ten visits.
lessons.exercise: Which experiment distinguishes these mechanisms when both appear during gallery navigation?
lessons.answer: Record allocations during a fixed scroll, then compare heap snapshots after repeated open-close cycles at the same resting screen. Inspect retaining paths and native bitmap memory as well as managed object counts.
